Question five. Walk me through BFS versus DFS: when do you choose each? Breadth-first search takes a queue, level by level. Depth-first takes a stack and follows one path down. Node A leads to B and C, and both lead to D. Breadth-first visits A, B, C, D; depth-first, A, B, D, then C. Choose BFS for shortest paths in an unweighted graph: it reaches each node first by the fewest edges. DFS for cycle detection, topological sort and backtracking. Memory decides it too. On a full binary tree of a million nodes, BFS holds the widest level, five hundred twenty-four thousand nodes; DFS holds one path, twenty. And make the queue a deck, a double-ended queue. Popping a Python list's front shifts everything behind it: two hundred seventy-five billion moves here. A deck pops either end in constant time.

Question six. How does a priority queue differ from a regular queue? A queue serves in arrival order. A priority queue serves the most urgent first, as in a scheduler or Dijkstra's algorithm. Keep a list sorted, most urgent at the end, and a pop is instant, but at a million items an insert shifts half a million on average. An unsorted list inserts instantly and scans to pop. A heap does both in log n, each parent at least as urgent as its children. A million items make twenty levels, so a push or pop moves at most nineteen; a peek is constant. The follow-up: building a heap is linear, not n log n, since most nodes sit near the bottom. For a million items arriving least urgent first, heapify takes one and a half million comparisons; pushed one at a time, eighteen million.
